tours.title: Luxor Highlights from Hurghada: Karnak, Luxor Temple & the Valley of the Kings
tours.description: Cross the desert from the Red Sea to ancient Thebes for a day among Karnak, Luxor Temple, the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Hatshepsut, with a licensed Egyptologist and never more than eight travellers.
included: Air-conditioned minivan, never more than 8 travellers
Entrance tickets: Karnak, Luxor Temple, Valley of the Kings (3 tombs), Temple of Hatshepsut
notIncluded: Optional tickets: Tutankhamun, Seti I and Nefertari tombs
whatToBring: Cash for lunch and optional tombs
A light layer for the early start

tours.overviewHtml:
From a sunbed on the Red Sea, Luxor can feel like a rumour — the greatest open-air museum on earth, somewhere beyond the mountains to the west. It is closer than it looks. Two hundred and ninety kilometres of desert road separate your hotel from the Nile, and this day crosses them before breakfast so that you can spend the heart of the day where ancient Thebes once stood, and be back in Hurghada by bedtime.

It is a long day, and we would rather say so plainly than pretend otherwise: roughly four hours of driving each way, bracketing about six hours among the temples and tombs. What those six hours hold is the reason people cross the desert. On the East Bank, the vast temple city of Karnak and the riverside Luxor Temple, where the living worshipped. On the West Bank, where the dead were laid to rest, the painted royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings, the terraced Temple of Hatshepsut against its cliff, and the two seated giants of the Colossi of Memnon.

This is a small-group shared departure — a mixed group of travellers from different hotels and different countries, one air-conditioned minivan, one licensed Egyptologist guide, and never more than eight of you. Sawa means "together," and a day this long is better in good company: the drive passes faster, the stories are shared, and the price comes down as the group grows. Your seat is held the moment you reserve, and nothing is charged until the date confirms.

Good to Know Before You Go

It starts before dawn. Pickup is around 5:00 AM. Ask your hotel for a breakfast box the night before — most Red Sea resorts will prepare one — and bring it with you for the road.

Wear comfortable shoes. Karnak is enormous, the Valley of the Kings involves slopes and steps inside the tombs, and Hatshepsut's temple is approached by long ramps. Supportive footwear makes the difference between a good day and a sore one.

Sun protection matters. Hat, sunglasses and sunscreen — the West Bank in particular offers little shade, and even in winter the midday sun is strong.

Bring cash for extras. Three tombs are included in your Valley of the Kings ticket. The tombs of Tutankhamun and Seti I carry separate tickets sold on site, as does the tomb of Nefertari in the Valley of the Queens. Your guide will tell you honestly whether they are worth it for you.

Carry your passport. The road between the Red Sea and the Nile Valley passes police checkpoints, and your guide may need to show the group's documents.

Dress light, but pack a layer. Pre-dawn and the late-evening return can be cool from October to March, while the middle of the day is warm year-round.

Day 1 — Across the Desert to Thebes

The Shape of the Day

05:00 AM — Pickup in Hurghada Your driver collects you from your hotel in the dark. You meet your fellow travellers as the minivan fills, settle in, and sleep or watch the dawn come up over the Eastern Desert.

05:30 AM — The Desert Road South along the coast to Safaga, then west through the mountains and across the desert to the Nile. There is a comfort stop along the way. Arrival in Luxor is around 9:00 to 9:30 AM, depending on the checkpoints.

09:30 AM — Karnak Temple Your Egyptologist leads you through the avenue of ram-headed sphinxes, the Great Hypostyle Hall of 134 columns, the obelisks of Hatshepsut and Tuthmosis, and the sacred lake. About an hour and a half on site.

11:15 AM — Luxor Temple A short drive along the river to Karnak's elegant companion — the temple of Amenhotep III and Ramses II, with the restored Avenue of Sphinxes running from its gate back toward Karnak.

12:15 PM — Lunch Stop (optional) A break at a local restaurant on the way to the West Bank for anyone who would like a proper meal. Lunch is paid directly; your guide will steer you to somewhere reliable.

01:15 PM — Valley of the Kings Across the bridge to the West Bank and into the valley where the New Kingdom pharaohs were buried. Your ticket admits you to three of the tombs open that day; your guide briefs you outside, as guiding inside the tombs is not permitted.

03:00 PM — Temple of Hatshepsut The terraced mortuary temple of Egypt's great female pharaoh, set into the amphitheatre of cliffs at Deir el-Bahari. About forty-five minutes.

03:50 PM — Colossi of Memnon A short stop before the two seated statues of Amenhotep III, all that stands of what was once the largest temple in Thebes.

04:15 PM — The Return Drive Back across the desert as the light goes golden and then dark. A comfort stop on the way.

08:30 PM — Drop-off in Hurghada Arrival back at your hotel in the evening, in time for a late dinner.

Timings are a plan rather than a promise: checkpoints, the group's pace on site and the Luxor traffic all move them a little.

Karnak — The Temple That Kept Growing

Karnak is not one temple but a city of them, built, enlarged and rebuilt by some thirty pharaohs over two thousand years. Nothing prepares you for the scale: the precinct of Amun alone covers more ground than many ancient towns.

The approach is a corridor of ram-headed sphinxes, and then the pylons open onto the Great Hypostyle Hall — 134 sandstone columns, the tallest of them twenty-one metres high, so thick that a dozen people linking hands could not circle one. Your guide reads the walls for you: Seti I and Ramses II at war, the gods receiving offerings, the cartouches of kings who added a court here and a gateway there as if the temple were never meant to be finished.

What Karnak gives you, more than any single monument, is a sense of time. Standing beside the obelisk of Hatshepsut, you are looking at stone quarried in Aswan and raised here nearly three and a half thousand years ago — and the hall around it was already old when Rome was founded.

Luxor Temple — Where the Festival Ended

Luxor Temple sits in the middle of the modern town, close to the river, and its mood is quite different from Karnak's. Where Karnak sprawls, Luxor is composed: a long axis of courts and colonnades built largely by Amenhotep III and finished by Ramses II, whose colossal seated statues and lone surviving obelisk guard the entrance.

Once a year the statues of the gods travelled here from Karnak for the Opet festival, carried along the three-kilometre Avenue of Sphinxes that has now been excavated and reopened in its entirety. The temple has never really stopped being sacred: a Roman shrine was painted inside it, a mosque was built on top of it, and the mosque is still in use today, perched above the ancient floor level.

Your guide walks you through the layers — pharaonic, Roman, Christian, Islamic — and the temple becomes a short history of Egypt itself.

The Valley of the Kings — Painted Rooms Under the Rock

For five hundred years the pharaohs of the New Kingdom gave up the pyramid and chose instead to be buried in secret, in tombs cut deep into a dry valley behind the Theban cliffs. Sixty-odd tombs have been found there, and a handful are open on any given day.

Your ticket covers three of them. Inside, the corridors descend through chamber after chamber painted with the texts that were meant to guide the king through the underworld — the Book of Gates, the Amduat, the Litany of Ra — and the colours, protected from sunlight for three millennia, are startlingly fresh. Guides explain the tombs outside and then let you walk them at your own pace, which is as it should be: the silence is part of it.

Tutankhamun's small, famous tomb and the magnificent tomb of Seti I are separately ticketed. Neither is required to make the visit worthwhile, and your guide will give you a straight opinion on whether they are worth the extra for you.

Hatshepsut and the Colossi — The Monuments of the West Bank

The mortuary temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari is unlike anything else in Egypt: three broad terraces climbing by ramps into a bay of golden cliffs, as modern in its lines as it is ancient in its story. Hatshepsut ruled as pharaoh in her own right for two decades, sent a trading expedition to the land of Punt that is recorded in relief on these walls, and was then systematically erased from the monuments by her successor. The temple survived the erasure; the reliefs of Punt — the incense trees, the fat queen, the exotic fish — are among the most charming in Egypt.

On the way back to the river, the Colossi of Memnon rise out of the fields: two weathered seated statues of Amenhotep III, eighteen metres high, which once flanked the gate of the largest temple ever built in Thebes. The temple is gone; the Colossi have kept their post for thirty-four centuries. It is the right place to end — a last look at the scale of what was here before the long road home.

Returning to Hurghada

The drive back is quieter than the drive out. The group has shared a day now, and the desert outside turns from gold to violet to black as the minivan heads east toward the coast.

You arrive at your hotel in the evening with a long day behind you and a good deal to think about — a city of temples, a valley of painted tombs, and the knowledge that all of it was waiting just across the mountains the whole time. You did it in one day, and you did it sawa, together.

tours.title: Dendera & Abydos from Hurghada: the Far Temples Day Tour
tours.description: A day with the two best-preserved temples in Egypt — Hathor's painted temple at Dendera and the exquisite reliefs of Seti I at Abydos — reached directly across the desert from Hurghada in a small group with a licensed Egyptologist.
included: Air-conditioned minivan, never more than 8 travellers
Entrance tickets: Temple of Hathor at Dendera, Temple of Seti I at Abydos
whatToBring: A small torch or phone light for the crypts
tours.meetingPoint: Pickup from your hotel in Hurghada
tours.pickupNote: Pickup is around 5:30 AM from hotels in Hurghada. Tell us where you are staying when you reserve; El Gouna, Sahl Hasheesh, Makadi Bay and Soma Bay on request.

images.alt: The restored painted ceiling of the Temple of Hathor at Dendera
Hathor-headed columns in the hypostyle hall at Dendera
Carved reliefs on the ceiling at Dendera
The Osireion behind the Temple of Seti I at Abydos
Painted raised relief in the Temple of Seti I at Abydos

tours.overviewHtml:
Most visitors to Egypt never see Dendera or Abydos. They lie north of Luxor, off the usual cruise route, and the coaches rarely make the detour — which is exactly why the two best-preserved temples in the country are also two of the quietest. For a traveller based on the Red Sea the geography is kinder than it is for most: the desert road from Hurghada meets the Nile at Qena, and Dendera stands just across the river.

This day takes you there. First the Temple of Hathor at Dendera, almost intact to its roof, with a painted astronomical ceiling that has been cleaned back to its original blues and golds. Then north to Abydos, the holiest city of ancient Egypt, where the Temple of Seti I holds the finest raised reliefs ever carved and the famous King List that gave Egyptology its chronology. You will see both with a licensed Egyptologist, in a group that is never larger than eight, and you will very often have the halls to yourselves.

It is a full day on the road — around twelve hours door to door — but it is a day of two temples rather than six, with time to stand still in each. Sawa means "together," and the shared minivan is what makes a journey this far off the beaten path affordable: the more of you who join, the lower the price for everyone. Reserve a seat for free; nothing is charged until the date confirms.

Good to Know Before You Go

Early start. Pickup is around 5:30 AM. Ask your hotel for a breakfast box the evening before.

Bring a torch or use your phone light. The crypts at Dendera and some of the chapels at Abydos are dim, and a small light reveals the detail of the reliefs.

Comfortable shoes and sun protection. There are stairs to the roof at Dendera and long stretches of open ground at Abydos. Hat, sunglasses and sunscreen all earn their place.

Lunch is not included. There is a lunch stop at a local restaurant between the two temples for anyone who would like one, paid directly. Bring snacks if you would rather keep moving.

Carry your passport. The road crosses police checkpoints between the Red Sea and the Nile Valley.

Modest dress is appreciated. These are working rural towns, and covered shoulders and knees are the comfortable choice for everyone.

Day 1 — North to the Far Temples

The Shape of the Day

05:30 AM — Pickup in Hurghada Your driver collects you from your hotel before first light. The minivan gathers the rest of the group from their hotels and heads out of town.

06:00 AM — The Desert Road to Qena West across the Eastern Desert on the Qena road — roughly three hours, with a comfort stop — arriving at the Nile Valley where the river bends closest to the Red Sea.

09:00 AM — The Temple of Hathor, Dendera Across the river to Dendera for about an hour and three-quarters: the great hypostyle hall with its Hathor-headed columns, the restored ceiling, the crypts, the roof chapels and the famous zodiac.

10:45 AM — North to Abydos Along the edge of the cultivation, about an hour and a half through the villages and sugar-cane fields of Upper Egypt.

12:15 PM — Lunch Stop (optional) A break at a local restaurant near Abydos for anyone who would like to eat, paid directly.

01:00 PM — The Temple of Seti I, Abydos About an hour and a half among the finest reliefs in Egypt: the seven sanctuaries, the King List, and the mysterious Osireion behind the temple.

02:30 PM — The Return Drive Back to Qena and east across the desert as the afternoon cools, with a comfort stop.

06:00 PM — Drop-off in Hurghada Arrival at your hotel in the early evening, in good time for dinner.

Checkpoint timings on the desert road vary, and the day is planned with that in mind. Exact times may shift a little.

Dendera — The House of Hathor, Almost Whole

Dendera is the temple that shows you what the others once looked like. Built in the last centuries before Christ by the Ptolemies and finished under the Roman emperors, it was buried to its roof in sand and rubbish for most of the following two thousand years, and so it survived nearly complete — walls, ceilings, stairways, crypts, and the roof you can still walk on.

The first sight is the hypostyle hall, where twenty-four columns rise to capitals carved with the face of Hathor, goddess of love, music and joy, and where the ceiling has recently been cleaned of centuries of soot. The colour that emerged is astonishing: deep blue skies, the goddess Nut swallowing the sun each evening, the signs of the zodiac, the boats of the hours. Beyond lie the inner halls and the sanctuary, and beneath them the narrow crypts where the temple's treasures were kept, carved with the reliefs that the internet has made famous as the "Dendera light."

Climb the ceremonial staircase to the roof — the same route the priests took each New Year to carry Hathor's statue up to greet the sunrise — and you find the small chapel of Osiris and, in its ceiling, a copy of the Dendera zodiac. The original is in the Louvre; your guide will tell you how it got there.

Abydos — The City of Osiris

Abydos was to ancient Egypt what Mecca or Jerusalem is to their faiths: the burial place of Osiris, lord of the dead, and the place every Egyptian hoped to visit once before dying — or at least to be carried past in a model boat after. The kings of the First Dynasty were buried here; three thousand years later pilgrims were still coming.

The temple that Seti I built here, and his son Ramses II finished, is the jewel of the site. Its reliefs are carved in raised relief rather than cut into the stone, a slower and more expensive technique, and the result is the most refined sculpture of the New Kingdom: the king offering to the gods in profile so delicate that the muscles of a forearm and the folds of linen are legible from across the room, much of the colour still clinging to the walls.

Along one corridor is the Abydos King List — seventy-six cartouches of Seti's predecessors, in order, from Menes to himself. It leaves out the heretic Akhenaten and the female pharaoh Hatshepsut, and in doing so it tells you as much about Seti's politics as about Egypt's past. It also gave nineteenth-century scholars the framework on which the whole chronology of ancient Egypt was built.

Behind the temple lies the Osireion, a massive granite structure sunk below ground level and often half-flooded, built in a style so archaic that its date is still debated. It is the kind of place that makes a day trip feel like an expedition.

Returning to Hurghada

The drive back east is the quiet part of the day. The sugar-cane fields give way to the desert, the desert to the mountains, and the mountains, eventually, to the first glimpse of the sea.

You arrive at your hotel in the early evening having seen two temples that most people who visit Egypt never reach — in a small group, with a guide who knew them well, and for a price that only sharing the road makes possible. Sawa, together.

tours.title: Cairo by Car from Hurghada: Pyramids, Grand Egyptian Museum & the Citadel
tours.description: The pyramids in one day from the Red Sea: Giza and the Sphinx, the Grand Egyptian Museum with the complete Tutankhamun collection, the Citadel of Saladin and a taste of Khan el-Khalili — by shared minivan rather than coach, with a licensed Egyptologist.

tours.overviewHtml:
There are travellers who come to the Red Sea for the diving and the sun, and who would still never forgive themselves for flying home without having seen the pyramids. This day exists for them. It is the longest day Sawa runs out of Hurghada — around nineteen hours door to door, more than ten of them on the road — and we will not dress that up. What it buys you is a full day in Cairo without a hotel night and without an airport: the Giza Plateau and the Great Sphinx in the morning, the new Grand Egyptian Museum at midday, and the Citadel of Saladin and a taste of Khan el-Khalili in the afternoon, before the long run back to the coast.

We do it by car rather than by coach, and the difference is not small. A shared minivan of at most eight travellers leaves when you are ready, moves through Cairo traffic as a car can, stops where a coach cannot, and gives your Egyptologist a conversation instead of a microphone. It also means the morning drive is a little faster and the day a little less tiring than the bus version you may have been offered.

Sawa means "together." Everyone in the minivan has made the same calculation — one very long day for the chance to stand under the Great Pyramid — and the price of making it comes down for all of you as the group grows. Reserve a seat for free; nothing is charged until the date confirms.

Good to Know Before You Go

It is a 4:00 AM pickup. Order a breakfast box from your hotel the evening before. The first hours are in the dark, and most people sleep.

Comfortable shoes above all. The Giza Plateau is sandy and uneven, the Grand Egyptian Museum is vast, and the Citadel is a climb. You will walk a good deal.

Sun protection. The plateau has almost no shade. Hat, sunglasses, sunscreen and water for the morning.

Lunch is not included. There is a lunch stop at a local restaurant after the museum, paid directly. Your guide will suggest somewhere reliable and quick.

Bring cash and small change. For lunch, for the bazaar, for the optional camel ride at the panorama, and for the separately ticketed interior of the Great Pyramid if you want to go inside.

Passport in your bag. The Red Sea road has police checkpoints, and the museum may ask for identification at the gate.

Expect to be back late. Drop-off at your hotel is usually around 11:00 PM. Plan a lazy morning for the day after.

Day 1 — The Long Road to the Pyramids

The Shape of the Day

04:00 AM — Pickup in Hurghada Your driver collects you from your hotel before dawn. The minivan gathers the rest of the group and heads north out of town.

04:30 AM — The Red Sea Road North along the coast and then north-west across the Eastern Desert toward Cairo — about five hours, with a comfort stop around halfway. Sunrise comes somewhere over the desert.

09:30 AM — The Giza Plateau Straight to the pyramids before the heat and the crowds. Your Egyptologist walks you through the three pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, the panorama viewpoint where all three line up, and the story of how and why they were built.

11:00 AM — The Great Sphinx & the Valley Temple Down to the Sphinx and the granite temple beside it, where the body of Khafre was prepared for burial.

11:45 AM — The Grand Egyptian Museum A short drive to the museum beside the plateau for a guided visit of about two and a half hours: the Grand Staircase, the main galleries, and the complete collection of Tutankhamun, displayed together for the first time.

02:15 PM — Lunch Stop (optional) A proper meal at a local restaurant in Giza or central Cairo, paid directly.

03:30 PM — The Citadel of Saladin Across the city to the medieval fortress on the Muqattam spur: the alabaster Mosque of Muhammad Ali and the terrace view over the whole of Cairo to the pyramids you stood beneath that morning.

04:45 PM — Khan el-Khalili A short, guided walk into the old bazaar — long enough for a mint tea at El Fishawy and a look at the lanes of copper and lanterns, not long enough to get lost.

05:30 PM — The Return Drive Out of Cairo in the evening rush and south toward the coast, with a comfort stop.

11:00 PM — Drop-off in Hurghada Back at your hotel late in the evening.

Cairo's traffic and the museum's entry flow are the two variables; your guide builds the afternoon around them.

The Giza Plateau — Standing Under the Only Wonder Left

Of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, one is still standing, and you reach it at half past nine in the morning with the sun still low and the plateau still quiet. The Great Pyramid of Khufu was the tallest building on earth for nearly four thousand years. Up close it stops being a shape and becomes a mountain made by hand — more than two million blocks, each heavier than a car, laid with a precision that modern surveyors still find hard to explain.

Your guide takes you from the base of Khufu to the pyramid of Khafre, which keeps its cap of smooth casing stone, and the smaller pyramid of Menkaure, and then out to the panorama point in the desert where the three align and the camera finally has room for them. Along the way the myths are cleared away — no slaves, no aliens — and replaced with something better: the organised, well-fed, proud workforce whose own tombs and bakeries have been excavated beside the plateau.

Then down to the Sphinx. Seventy-three metres long and carved from a single outcrop of limestone, it has watched the sunrise from the foot of Khafre's causeway for four and a half thousand years, and it is smaller, stranger and more moving in person than any photograph suggests.

The Grand Egyptian Museum — Tutankhamun Comes Home

For a century, Egypt's greatest treasures were squeezed into a handsome but hopelessly overcrowded museum in central Cairo. The Grand Egyptian Museum was built to end that. It stands within sight of the pyramids, a vast wedge of stone and glass, and it opened in full at the end of 2025 as the largest archaeological museum in the world.

The visit begins under the eleven-metre colossus of Ramses II in the atrium and climbs the Grand Staircase, lined with statues of kings and gods, toward a window framing the pyramids themselves. Beyond lie the main galleries, arranged by period and theme, and at the heart of the building the complete tomb treasure of Tutankhamun — more than five thousand objects, including the golden mask, the nested shrines and the chariots, together in one place for the first time since they were taken out of the tomb in the 1920s.

A museum this size could swallow a week. Your Egyptologist keeps the visit to two and a half focused hours, choosing the galleries that matter and telling the stories that connect the objects to the plateau you have just walked.

The Citadel and Khan el-Khalili — Medieval Cairo in an Afternoon

From the pharaohs to the sultans. The Citadel was begun by Saladin in 1176 to defend Cairo from the Crusaders and remained the seat of Egypt's rulers for seven hundred years. Its crown is the Mosque of Muhammad Ali, built in the 1830s in the Ottoman style with its clustered domes and pencil minarets, its walls clad in alabaster, and from its terrace the whole of Cairo lies below you — the minarets of the old city in the foreground, the Nile beyond, and on a clear afternoon, the pyramids on the horizon.

Then down into the old city for a short walk through Khan el-Khalili, the bazaar that has traded on the same lanes since the fourteenth century. Your guide leads you through the spice and copper alleys to El Fishawy, the café that claims not to have closed in two hundred years, for a glass of mint tea before the road. It is a taste rather than a meal — but it is the right note on which to leave Cairo: alive, loud, and still trading.

Returning to Hurghada

The last stretch is the longest, and most of the group sleeps through it. Cairo's lights thin out behind you, the desert closes in, and somewhere after midnight-dark the first hotel signs of the coast appear.

You arrive back late, tired, and with the one thing you came for: you have stood under the Great Pyramid, looked the Sphinx in the eye, and seen the mask of Tutankhamun in its new home — all in a single day from the Red Sea, in a small group that shared the road. Sawa, together.

tours.title: Nubian Temples of Lake Nasser: Kalabsha, Beit el-Wali & Kertassi
tours.vehicle: Air-conditioned minivan (Toyota HiAce) + motor boat, max 8 travellers
tours.description: A half-day boat trip to the rescued temples of Lower Nubia on New Kalabsha island, just above the High Dam: the Roman-era Temple of Kalabsha, the painted rock-chapel of Beit el-Wali and the Kiosk of Kertassi, with a licensed Egyptologist.

Motor boat to New Kalabsha island and back
Hotel or cruise-berth pickup & drop-off in Aswan
Entrance tickets: Kalabsha, Beit el-Wali and Kertassi
whatToBring: Shoes with grip for the granite paths
A small torch or phone light
tours.meetingPoint: Pickup from your hotel or cruise berth in Aswan
tours.pickupNote: Pickup is around 8:00 AM from hotels and cruise berths in Aswan. Tell us your ship and berth when you reserve and we arrange the boat around it.

images.alt: A motor boat on the Nile at Aswan
The Nile and the granite islands at Aswan from above

tours.overviewHtml:
Just south of the High Dam, on a rocky island at the edge of Lake Nasser, stand three temples that almost nobody visits. They were not built here. When the dam was finished in the 1960s and the lake began to rise, the monuments of Lower Nubia were cut into blocks, carried out of the valley, and rebuilt on higher ground — Abu Simbel most famously, but also these: the great sandstone Temple of Kalabsha, the small painted rock-chapel of Beit el-Wali, and the graceful Kiosk of Kertassi, standing at the water's edge like a question mark.

Reaching them is part of the pleasure. A short drive from your Aswan hotel to the dock above the dam, a fifteen-minute crossing by motor boat with the lake opening around you, and then two and a half hours on an island you will very likely share with no one but your own group. The temples are complete, the carvings crisp, the setting — bare granite, blue water, open desert — as Nubian as anything in Egypt.

It is a half day, back at your hotel for lunch, and it slots easily beside a Nile cruise departure or an afternoon at Philae. Sawa means "together," and the boat and the guide are what the group shares: the more travellers who join the date, the lower the price per person. Reserve a seat for free; nothing is charged until the date confirms.

Good to Know Before You Go

A morning out of the sun's worst. Pickup is around 8:00 AM and you are back by about 1:00 PM — before the Aswan afternoon heat.

Sun protection. The island has no shade at all. Hat, sunglasses, sunscreen and water.

Shoes with grip. The landing stage and the paths between the temples are rough granite.

Bring a small torch or your phone light. The painted reliefs of Beit el-Wali are inside a rock-cut chapel and reward a closer look.

Camera ready on the boat. The crossing gives the best view of the temples, with the dam behind them and the lake ahead.

Staying on a cruise boat? Tell us your ship and berth when you reserve and we will arrange the pickup around it.

Day 1 — Across the Water to New Kalabsha

The Shape of the Day

08:00 AM — Pickup in Aswan Your driver and Egyptologist collect you from your hotel or cruise berth. The minivan gathers the rest of the group and heads south through town.

08:30 AM — The Dock Above the High Dam A short drive past the dam to the landing on the lake shore, where the motor boat is waiting.

08:45 AM — The Crossing About fifteen minutes across the water to New Kalabsha island, with the temples growing larger ahead of you and the dam receding behind.

09:00 AM — The Temple of Kalabsha The main event: about an hour and a quarter in the largest free-standing temple of Lower Nubia — the causeway, the pylon, the courtyard, the hypostyle hall and the sanctuary, with its reliefs of Roman emperors dressed as pharaohs.

10:20 AM — Beit el-Wali A few minutes' walk to the small rock-cut temple of Ramses II, whose painted battle scenes keep much of their colour. About twenty-five minutes.

10:50 AM — The Kiosk of Kertassi Down to the water for the little Roman-era kiosk, its Hathor-headed columns framing the lake — the closing photograph of the morning.

11:15 AM — The Boat Back Return crossing to the dock and the drive back into Aswan.

12:30 PM — Drop-off Back at your hotel or ship in time for lunch, with the afternoon free.

Kalabsha — Rome's Temple to a Nubian God

The Temple of Kalabsha is the largest and best preserved of the rescued monuments after Abu Simbel, and the surprise is who built it. Though it stands on a site sacred since the New Kingdom, the temple you walk through was raised under the Roman emperor Augustus, around 30 BC, in honour of Mandulis — a Nubian sun god whom the Egyptians had adopted and the Romans were happy to inherit.

The approach is a long stone causeway from the water, then a pylon, an open court, and a hypostyle hall whose column capitals are carved with lotus and palm. On the walls, Augustus and later emperors appear in the full regalia of pharaohs, offering to Mandulis, Isis and Osiris — a Roman emperor who never set foot in Egypt, drawn as the son of Ra. Inscriptions from later centuries are scattered through the temple: a decree in Greek expelling pigs from the precinct, a Meroitic king's victory text, Christian crosses from when the sanctuary became a church.

The whole building — some thirteen thousand blocks — was dismantled by a German team in 1962–63 and rebuilt here, forty kilometres from its original site. Your guide points out the seams.

Beit el-Wali and Kertassi — The Small Temples

A short walk from Kalabsha, the rock-cut temple of Beit el-Wali is older and more intimate. Ramses II had it carved early in his reign, and the forecourt reliefs are a comic-strip of his campaigns: Nubians bringing tribute of leopards, giraffes and gold; the king in his chariot scattering Libyans and Syrians; princes leading prisoners. Inside, in the vestibule and sanctuary, the colour is remarkably preserved — reds, yellows and blues on scenes of the king before the gods of the cataract.

The Kiosk of Kertassi is smaller still: six columns and a lintel, rebuilt at the water's edge, two of them with the face of Hathor on their capitals. It once stood at the entrance to a sandstone quarry that supplied the temples of Nubia, and it is thought to have been dedicated to Isis. It is a slight building, but in its setting — granite, water, and the empty desert beyond — it makes the morning's point better than anything else: that a whole landscape of temples was lifted out of a drowning valley and set down again, stone by stone, so that you could stand here.

Returning to Aswan

The boat carries you back across the lake toward the long wall of the dam, and the minivan returns you to your hotel or your ship with the afternoon still ahead.

In four and a half hours you have seen three temples that most Nile travellers sail past without knowing they are there, in a group small enough to hear every word and quiet enough to hear the water. Sawa, together.
